title: Ewan the Seal and the Starry Symphony
markdown:
The old observatory had dressed itself for a public viewing night. Stars waited above the dome like scattered diamonds. Music was meant to flow below like a gentle river. At the heart of that arrangement stood Ewan, a seal of considerable skill and even more considerable anxiety.

Ewan restored pianos. He coaxed forgotten melodies from the wooden souls of old instruments, and he believed, with all his whiskered heart, that true joy was a matter of careful planning. “A harmonious arrangement,” he murmured, polishing a keyboard with the softest cloth, “that is the secret to finding delight.”

Tonight he would unveil a grand piano he had lovingly restored. The demonstration was meant to prove a stubborn point. Meticulous preparation was not the enemy of fun. It was the foundation on which good times were built.

Beside him, darting through the gathering crowd like a streak of quicksilver, was Theo the otter. Theo had once been Ewan’s rival. Tonight he served as the evening’s unofficial greeter, and he treated the job as an invitation to charming disorder. “Welcome, welcome, everyone,” he chirped, his voice like bubbling brook water, ushering guests towards the telescopes. His sleek dark fur shone under the warm observatory lights. His bowtie was flamboyant enough to start a rumour.

Ewan watched him, a faint ripple of unease disturbing his calm. “If this is going to be a disaster,” Ewan muttered, his gaze flicking to that bowtie, “it is certainly going to be an unusually well-dressed one.”

The air buzzed. Hushed whispers about nebulae mixed with the faint clatter of Theo orchestrating a lively game of find-the-constellation. Children pointed at the dome. A volunteer swung a telescope toward Cassiopeia and then, with equal confidence, toward a bright streetlamp. Someone asked whether the Milky Way had a favourite star. Ewan clutched his notes. Each page was numbered and colour-coded, with a tiny star beside the moment he meant to lift the fallboard and reveal the restored soundboard, pale as cream. He was ready. Or, at least, his plan was.

He set his flippers on the keys for a gentle prelude. A small curious hand tugged at his sleeve. A child no older than five looked up, eyes shining with pure wonder. “Mr Seal,” she whispered, “can the piano make the stars sing?”

Ewan offered a tight polite smile. His rehearsed introduction vanished like a dropped page. Before he could find a proper answer, Theo swooped in with theatrical grandeur. “Of course, little one. Every single note played tonight sends a tiny musical greeting straight to the heavens.”

This was not in the plan. Ewan’s brow furrowed, a small crease appearing between his thoughtful eyes. Theo was already encouraging the child to hum a simple tune, which he then attempted to mimic with a toy kazoo. The kazoo made a valiant, slightly soggy sound. The audience chuckled. Attention slid from the polished piano to the charming chaotic duet unfolding beside it.

Ewan’s heart sank with a quiet thud. His moment, his carefully crafted display of skill, was slipping away on a tide of unscripted merriment. The old rivalry with Theo surfaced like a remembered bruise. He wanted order. Precision. A controlled demonstration. Instead he had this: a delightful, spontaneous, completely unplanned moment of shared joy.

The child hummed again, louder now, and two more children joined her. Theo conducted them with the kazoo as if it were a royal sceptre. Ewan’s numbered notes trembled in his flipper. He could still stop it. He could clear his throat, return to page one, and salvage the prelude.

Then Theo turned, dark eyes twinkling with genuine warmth. “Ewan,” he said, the showmanship falling away, “your piano is truly magnificent. But perhaps, just perhaps, it needs a chorus.” He gestured to the children, who were waiting with bright faces to contribute their own little hums and giggles.

Ewan looked at the gleaming piano. He looked at the expectant faces. He looked at Theo, his old rival, and saw not an opponent but a collaborator, a fellow spirit in this celebration of wonder. He took a deep breath. The clean scent of old wood and starlight filled his lungs. He nodded, a small decisive nod.

He began to play. His flippers moved with practised grace, but the music now carried a new warmth, a spark from the joyous energy around him. The children’s pure hums wove themselves like silver threads into the melody. Theo, with a dramatic flourish, provided a gentle rhythmic splash from a nearby bucket of water, which somehow harmonised with the piano. One child kept time by tapping the paper crown later found beside the ledger. The audience clapped along, smiles wide and utterly genuine. The restored instrument sang not only with Ewan’s skill, but with the collective spirit of the night.

A telescope turned. Someone claimed a high note had found Orion. Whether that was true hardly mattered. The dome felt less like a lecture hall and more like a shared instrument, wood and water and breath agreeing on a tempo no colour-coded page had listed.

Later, as the last guests departed with lingering wonder still on their faces, Ewan found his ledger book, where he had logged every detail of the restoration. Beside it, forgotten in the flurry, lay a brightly coloured paper crown from the children’s game. It was a small thing, a discarded treasure. Under the dimming observatory lights its faded colours seemed to glow. He had planned for perfection and found something richer in the spirit of collaboration.

And so Ewan learned that careful planning may lay a foundation, but joy grows brightest when others are allowed to add their voices, even if the evening begins with a slightly dishevelled otter and a very well-planned piano.
characters: Ewan (seal piano restorer who polishes keys for harmony), Theo (an otter of charming disorder and a flamboyant bowtie)
